html:
A large silver coin of Athens, worth four drachmas, struck from the late 6th century BCE. It shows the head of the goddess Athena on one side and her owl, an olive sprig and the letters of the city's name on the other.

The silver came from the mines of Laurion in Attica, and after the silver strike of 483 BCE Athens could mint huge numbers. The coins paid the rowers of the fleet and the building of the Parthenon, and the tribute of the Delian League flowed back into them. Because their weight and purity were reliable, they were accepted across the Mediterranean and the Near East, and people in Arabia, Egypt and elsewhere made copies.

Owls were so common that "bringing owls to Athens" meant doing something pointless, a joke used by Aristophanes. The coin followed the first coins of Lydia and Aegina, and its owl appears today on the Greek one euro coin.
